title: Racecraft and Strategy
intro: A fast lap on an empty track is only part of racing. In a race the driver shares the track with other cars, has to get past some and keep others behind, must look after the tyres and fuel over many laps, and may need to stop in the pits. Racecraft is the skill of wheel-to-wheel driving; strategy is the planning of the whole race. Both apply in the same way in real series and in online racing games.

blocks.text: Qualifying sets the starting grid, usually by each driver's best single lap. Starting further forward avoids traffic and the risk of the first corner, so a good qualifying lap is often worth more than a fast race pace on tracks where overtaking is hard. Starts are either standing (cars stationary on the grid, released by lights going out) or rolling (cars moving behind a pace or safety car). On a standing start, the launch is a balance between wheelspin and bogging the engine; on a rolling start, the leader controls the pace and must not accelerate before the start zone. The first lap is where most incidents happen: the aim is to gain positions without throwing the race away in the first corner.

A car punches a hole in the air, leaving a region of lower pressure and slower air behind it. A car following closely through that wake has less drag and can go faster on the straight: the slipstream, or draft. The usual pass is to follow closely out of a corner, slipstream down the straight, pull out of the wake at the end and use the extra speed to get alongside before the braking zone. Some series add an overtaking aid, such as a drag reduction system (DRS), used in Formula 1 from 2011 to 2025, which opened a rear-wing flap for a car within one second of the car ahead, or a push-to-pass button with a limited supply of extra power.

items: The inside line into the braking zone is the usual place to pass: the car on the inside has the right to the apex once it is substantially alongside.
Braking later than the car ahead (an outbraking move or dive) works only if the attacker can still make the corner. A pass that can only end by hitting the other car is not a pass.
The switchback or cross-over: when the defender takes the inside, the attacker goes wide, turns in later, and uses a better exit to drive back past on the following straight.
Around the outside: possible but risky, because the car on the inside controls the exit. Best where the following corner turns the other way, so the outside car becomes the inside car.
Setting up a pass: a driver who is slightly faster through one corner can stay close, push the defender into defending, then pass where the defender's compromised line costs them exit speed.

Most series allow one defensive change of direction on a straight; moving back towards the racing line to take the corner is allowed if it leaves the attacker room. Moving in the braking zone, or weaving to break the slipstream, is penalised.
Covering the inside: moving to the inside before the braking zone forces the attacker to try the outside. It costs some exit speed, so it is a trade.

Leave room: once an attacker has a meaningful overlap (commonly, their front wheels alongside the defender's rear wheels or further), the defender must leave at least a car's width at the edge of the track.
A defender who is clearly slower usually loses less time by letting a car through cleanly than by fighting and losing pace to the cars behind as well.
Be predictable. Sudden moves and unexpected braking cause most accidents.
After a spin, wait for a gap before rejoining, and rejoin away from the racing line. In games this matters as much as in real life: an unsafe rejoin is the most common cause of crashes online.
Lapping: a car being lapped should hold its line and let the faster car choose where to pass, or move off the line in a safe place. Blue flags tell the slower car it is about to be lapped.
Multi-class racing: in endurance races, the faster class usually does the passing and the slower class holds its line.
Online racing services often rate drivers on both results and safety (incident points), and match drivers of similar ratings. A clean race usually does more for the rating than a fast but messy one.

blocks.text: Marshals show flags to give drivers information they cannot see. The meanings are close to universal in real racing (the FIA's International Sporting Code sets them for most international series) and most racing games copy them.

items: Green: the track is clear; racing may begin or resume.
Yellow: danger ahead; slow down, no overtaking. Double yellow: slow down a lot and be ready to stop.
Red: the session is stopped; slow down and return to the pit lane.
Blue: a faster car is about to lap you; let it through.
White: a slow vehicle, such as a recovery truck, is on the track ahead (in some American series, it means the last lap).
Black: the driver shown must return to the pits; usually disqualification.
Black and white diagonal: a warning for unsporting driving or track-limit abuse.
Black with an orange disc (meatball): the car has a mechanical problem and must pit.
Red and yellow stripes: slippery surface (oil, water or debris) ahead.
Chequered: the end of the race or session.
Safety car (SC) and full-course yellow: all cars slow down behind a safety car, or to a set speed, while an incident is cleared; gaps close up and a cheap pit stop may become possible.

blocks.text: Over a stint, tyres lose grip as they wear and heat up, so lap times rise (degradation). Fuel burns off, so the car gets lighter and faster. Strategy balances the two: how many times to stop, which tyre compound to use for each stint, and when to stop.

items: Stops: each pit stop costs the time to drive down the pit lane at its speed limit plus the stationary time, often 20 to 30 seconds in total. A stop is worth making when fresh tyres gain more than that over the following laps.
The undercut: stopping a lap before a rival, then using the grip of new tyres to set a faster out lap, so that when the rival stops they come out behind.
The overcut: staying out longer than a rival, when the rival's new tyres take time to warm up or they come out into traffic.
Tyre management: saving tyres by avoiding wheelspin and slides, being gentle in the corners that wear them most, and not chasing the car in front through its dirty air.
Fuel saving: lifting off the throttle a little before the braking zone (lift and coast) uses less fuel and takes heat out of the brakes, at a small cost in lap time.
Weather: switching to wet or intermediate tyres at the right lap can win a race outright; too early or too late loses it.

blocks.title: Is one more stop worth it?
blocks.text: A pit stop costs 22 seconds. On new tyres a car laps 1.5 s faster than on old ones at first, and the advantage falls by 0.1 s each lap after that. With 20 laps to go, does an extra stop pay?
blocks.hint: Add up the gain lap by lap: 1.5 + 1.4 + 1.3 + ... for up to 20 laps, but the gain cannot fall below zero.
solution: The gain is 1.5 s, then 0.1 s less each lap until it reaches zero after 15 laps, so the total is 1.5 + 1.4 + ... + 0.1 = 12 seconds.
That is less than the 22 seconds the stop costs, so the extra stop does not pay unless a safety car makes the stop cheaper, or the old tyres are about to fail.
blocks.answer: No: it gains about 12 s and costs 22 s
